The Senate Rejects the Treaty of Versailles
summary: The defeat of President Woodrow Wilson’s plan for a League of Nations highlighted the power of the Senate and the dangers of refusing to compromise.

ai.sum: A historical CFR piece recounts the US Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles and Wilson's League of Nations.

brief.summary: The authors, writing as a CFR retrospective on the 1919 Senate rejection of the Treaty of Versailles, trace how Woodrow Wilson moved from neutrality to war and then to championing a League of Nations as the centrepiece of the peace. They argue that Wilson's domestic political missteps, including his appeal to voters before the 1918 midterms, cost Democrats control of Congress and hardened Republican opposition. They describe Senate chair Henry Cabot Lodge delaying the treaty and drafting fourteen reservations, while Wilson refused to compromise and then suffered a stroke. The piece characterises the debate as one over the form of internationalism rather than a simple isolationist-versus-internationalist split. The authors conclude that US non-participation weakened the League and that the lesson of the episode shaped American foreign policy for the following eight decades. It is a historical essay with no explicit policy recommendations.
brief.argument: The Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles resulted from Wilson's refusal to compromise and his domestic political miscalculations, and it shaped US engagement with the world for decades.

title: Putin didn’t get his Yalta, but he’s happy nonetheless
summary: In the Shenzhen summit with Trump and Xi, Putin got the propaganda victory he wanted without having to make any concessions on Ukraine. The post Putin didn’t get his Yalta, but he’s happy nonetheless appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Commentary says Putin gained a propaganda win at the Shenzhen summit with Trump and Xi without conceding on Ukraine.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Shenzhen trilateral summit among Putin, Xi and Trump, though far from the Yalta-style gathering Putin had wanted, gave him a valuable image of normalcy and friendship with the US president. They read the joint declaration as tailored to Russian concerns: its language on the ICC, nuclear war, oil flows and the UN serves Putin's interests, while Ukraine is not mentioned. They see Xi placing Putin as a junior partner, but argue that Putin is nonetheless content. The authors contend that Putin gains a political signal to the Russian elite that he cannot be isolated, and that Trump's reluctance to sanction Russian oil exports effectively secures his economy. They conclude that Putin is not moving toward a peace settlement and sees no reason to compromise with a US administration he regards as a lame duck.
brief.argument: Putin gained a major symbolic and economic win from the Shenzhen summit without making any concessions on Ukraine or peace.

title: What the Trump-Putin-Xi meeting actually achieved
summary: Our experts unpack what Trump, Xi, and Putin gained from their summit and what their declaration means for the global order. The post What the Trump-Putin-Xi meeting actually achieved appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council experts analysed the gains and implications of a Trump, Xi and Putin summit and its declaration.

brief.summary: The authors, Atlantic Council experts, argue that the Trump-Putin-Xi meeting in Shenzhen was mostly image and little substance. They say Beijing shaped the narrative through a four-point "declaration toward peace". They see one modest gain in the reaffirmation that a nuclear war cannot be won, and that China's inclusion could be built on. They warn that China's nuclear build-up continues, and that the leaders' stance on the ICC threatens its foundations and moves away from US support for accountability. They read the UN reform call as serving Beijing's push against Western values, and the oil production point as likely to favour Russia by undermining sanctions. Xi gains a picture of China in the driver's seat, Putin gains equal great-power standing, and Trump misses a chance to advance a free-world agenda. The authors also contrast the summit with the Berlin Coalition of the Willing meeting on Ukraine.
brief.argument: The authors argue that the Trump-Putin-Xi summit was all image and little substance, with its declaration advancing Beijing's narrative, weakening ICC accountability, and easing pressure on Russian oil sales.
recommendations: The US president should back the Berlin Coalition of the Willing meeting rather than pursue photo opportunities with Putin.
Build on the nuclear-war reaffirmation by bringing China further into nuclear-arms discussions.
UN reform should promote accountability and equal voices among states rather than consolidate great-power power.
brief.turkey: The summit's signals on Russian oil sanctions and great-power bargaining over Ukraine bear on Türkiye's energy and Black Sea calculations, though the piece does not address Türkiye directly.

title: The US didn’t have a strong plan for the Shenzhen summit. It showed.
summary: The leaders’ trilateral meeting in Shenzhen ended up benefiting Beijing and Moscow at the expense of Washington. The post The US didn’t have a strong plan for the Shenzhen summit. It showed. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Analysis says the Shenzhen trilateral summit benefited Beijing and Moscow at Washington's expense.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the United States went into the Shenzhen trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin without a clear plan, and so was used to lend legitimacy to China and Russia. They say Trump rests his approach on three misconceptions: that Xi and Putin like him, that Chinese pageantry benefits Washington, and that Sino-Russian ties will loosen because they 'like Trump'. The summit produced a four-point declaration that, in their reading, mostly serves Chinese and Russian aims, such as UN reform, more fossil fuel production and immunity for heads of state from the ICC. The one point they think Washington added, a dialogue on nuclear risk, is in their view empty and buys Beijing time while its arsenal grows. They conclude that the US left with nothing concrete, while the images will shape how allies view their ties with Washington, and they urge focus on partners who want to work with the US rather than on splitting China and Russia.
brief.argument: The US walked into the Shenzhen summit without a strong plan, and the trilateral format let Beijing and Moscow gain image and substance at American expense.
recommendations: Enter leader-level meetings with authoritarian rivals only with a clear, specific plan and concrete objectives
Seek tangible commitments, such as reliable rare earth supply for US companies, rather than accepting pageantry
Stop spending effort trying to drive China and Russia apart and focus on allies who want to work with the US
Treat empty dialogue offers on nuclear risk as stalling tactics unless they come with verifiable steps
brief.turkey: The summit's images and the Sino-Russian-US framing bear on how Ankara reads US reliability and great-power bargaining, though the piece does not address Türkiye directly.

title: Lessons from Brazil and Peru on how to build AI-ready institutions across Latin America
summary: Brazil and Peru offer early blueprints for AI regulation in Latin America: one for building regulatory institutions before legislation is in place, and another for turning AI laws into effective governance. The post Lessons from Brazil and Peru on how to build AI-ready institutions across Latin America appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council examines how Brazil and Peru are building AI regulatory institutions and governance frameworks.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Latin American AI governance is colliding with institutional limits, since imported European-style regulatory models must be translated into clear authority, operational capacity and accountability at home. They compare two cases. Brazil is building institutional architecture before its general AI law is settled, strengthening its data protection authority into a full regulator and showing how the electoral court acted as an interim AI regulator in the 2026 elections. Peru has passed a general AI law and implementing regulations that divide enforcement among existing bodies, but they warn its agencies may lack budget and bandwidth to enforce. The authors frame three tests for AI readiness: clear authority, capacity to absorb mandates, and mechanisms to detect and correct failure. They conclude that regulation is only one part of readiness and must be developed alongside institutions.
brief.argument: Latin American AI governance will be hollow unless institutional authority, operational capacity and accountability are built alongside regulation, as the Brazil and Peru cases show.
recommendations: Clearly define the processes, roles and responsibilities of actors across the data lifecycle, drawing on the OAS MIGDIA framework before comprehensive AI law exists.
Empower existing judicial institutions to act as interim regulators for specific risks while an independent AI regulator is established.
Set up efficient inter-agency communication channels and sector-based enforcement responsibilities to ensure accountability.
Scale institutional resources as regulatory responsibilities expand, and build transparency through reporting indicators on digital government capacity.

title: Dispatch from Manama: The Iran war is not over for Bahrain
summary: A recent visit to Bahrain offers a window into the ongoing tensions with Iran and diplomatic maneuvering among Gulf nations. The post Dispatch from Manama: The Iran war is not over for Bahrain appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: A visit to Bahrain describes ongoing tensions with Iran and diplomatic manoeuvring among Gulf states.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Iran war is not over despite Trump's claim that it is militarily effectively over, pointing to Iranian drone attacks on Bahrain and a third US carrier strike group entering the region. They describe a Gulf that no longer acts as a single bloc, with governments entering an "age of agency" and hedging as they doubt US reliability. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Oman and Kuwait are each portrayed pursuing different strategies, from accommodation with Iran to new partnerships with Türkiye and Pakistan. Bahrain is presented as having deepened its alignment with Washington despite its vulnerabilities, a relationship the authors say is under-recognised and taken for granted in US policy circles.
brief.argument: The Iran war remains live and Gulf states are diverging in strategy, with each hedging or acting on its own as US reliability is questioned, while Bahrain has doubled down on its US alignment.
recommendations: Washington should give Bahrain and the Gulf greater attention, including senior engagement at forums such as the Manama Dialogue
Gulf states should keep hedging through varied partnerships given doubts about US dependability

title: Kyiv’s partners should prioritize Ukraine’s domestic drone production
summary: Ukrainian long-range drone strikes have reduced Russian oil refining output by around 45 percent in the past few weeks, Reuters reports. Kyiv's partners should build on this success and prioritize funding for Ukraine's domestic drone industry, writes Leonid Baratz. The post Kyiv’s partners should prioritize Ukraine’s domestic drone production appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Commentary argues Ukraine's partners should fund its domestic drone industry after long-range strikes cut Russian refining output.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Ukraine's long-range drone strikes have sharply cut Russian oil refining, with a 45 percent drop cited from Reuters and a higher figure from Zelenskyy. Their central puzzle is why there are not more such drones, and they answer that money, not engineering or industrial capacity, is the constraint. They say Ukraine's defence sector now has large excess capacity, with officials estimating that much of it is unused or uncontracted, while Kyiv spends about 40 percent of GDP on defence, largely on personnel. They highlight the 'Danish model', in which donors pay Ukrainian manufacturers directly, and argue that Ukrainian drones are cheap and combat-tested. They acknowledge corruption concerns and call for audits, and note dependence on imported engines and electronics, which joint ventures with European partners could address.
brief.argument: Money, rather than industrial capacity, is what limits Ukraine's drone output, so Kyiv's partners should fund Ukrainian domestic production.
recommendations: Direct donor funding to Ukrainian defence manufacturers through the Danish model
Pair funding with audits and transparency safeguards against corruption
Form joint ventures with European partners to secure imported components and move production out of Russian strike range
Channel part of NATO allies' increased defence budgets into Ukrainian production
